deck: 30 Thinking in Java::01 Introduction to Objects

cards.front: In Thinking in Java, what is the problem space and what is the solution space?
cards.back: Problem space: where the problem lives (the business). Solution space: where you implement it (the machine)
cards.extra: The book's argument is that OOP shrinks the distance between them — you model the business's own vocabulary instead of the computer's structures, so the code reads like the problem.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::06 Basics of OOP

cards.front: According to Alan Kay's five characteristics, what is a program?
cards.back: A bunch of objects telling each other what to do by sending messages
cards.extra: A message is just a request to call a method on a particular object. Java makes that literal: shape.draw() is a message to the shape object.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::06 Basics of OOP

cards.front: What is the most important distinguishing characteristic of a class?
cards.back: The set of messages you can send it — its interface
cards.extra: Two classes with the same interface are interchangeable from the caller's point of view. That is why the book introduces interface before implementation detail.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::06 Basics of OOP

cards.front: Booch's one-sentence definition of an object?
cards.back: An object has state, behaviour and identity
cards.extra: State = internal data, behaviour = methods, identity = a distinct address in memory. Two objects with identical fields are still two objects, which is exactly the == versus equals distinction.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::06 Basics of OOP

cards.front: What does it mean that every object has an interface?
cards.back: It is the set of requests you are allowed to make of it — its public methods
cards.extra: The interface is the contract; the implementation is how it happens. Callers code against the interface, so the implementation can change underneath them.

cards.front: Why does thinking in Java insist on hiding the implementation?
cards.back: So the implementer can change it without breaking every caller, and so clients cannot depend on internals
cards.extra: Hiding gives two things at once: a boundary nobody can reach past, and the freedom to rewrite. Without it, every field is part of your public API forever.

cards.back: An is-a relationship: the derived type is a subtype of the base type
cards.extra: The derived class keeps the base interface and may add methods and fields. It also inherits the base's implementation, which is the part that becomes a maintenance liability if the relationship is wrong.

cards.back: Replacing a base-class method with a subclass version that has the same signature
cards.extra: The book stresses that the subclass must keep the exact signature, otherwise you have overloaded rather than replaced it — a distinction that decides which method runs at runtime.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::14 Static vs Dynamic Binding

cards.front: What mechanism lets one method that takes a Shape work with Circle and Triangle?
cards.back: Polymorphism — the call is bound to the object's actual type at runtime
cards.extra: The call site knows only the base type; late binding picks the derived implementation. That is what makes doSomething(shape) extensible without editing it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::14 Static vs Dynamic Binding

cards.front: What is upcasting and why is it safe?
cards.back: Treating a derived object as its base type — always safe, so no cast is needed
cards.extra: Every Circle IS-A Shape, so any base method exists on the derived object. The reverse direction needs a cast and can fail, which is where ClassCastException comes from.

cards.front: Why does Java need container classes rather than plain arrays?
cards.back: Containers hold any number of objects of a given type and expand as needed
cards.extra: ArrayList<Shape> shapes can grow while the program runs, and it enforces the element type. Arrays fix their length at creation and cannot grow.

cards.front: Where do Java objects live, and what does that make their lifetime?
cards.back: On the heap; they live until no reference reaches them
cards.extra: Creation is new, destruction is the garbage collector's decision. The book calls this the one place where you lose control compared with C++, and where most leaks disappear.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle

cards.front: What does exception handling buy you, in Einstein's framing from this chapter?
cards.back: Error handling separated from the normal path — reported where it can actually be handled
cards.extra: Errors are thrown to a handler that knows what to do, instead of every call returning a status code. The normal flow stays readable; the recovery code lives in one place.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: Why is concurrency described as a fundamental difficulty, not a feature?
cards.back: Multiple threads act on shared resources at the same time, so correctness depends on coordination
cards.extra: The classic picture is many tasks running on one machine, each needing the same memory. Without a locking or message discipline, results depend on timing — the bugs are rare and hard to reproduce.
